query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: The single intervention of adding a thin, oxidation-resistant coating (e.g., Al2O3 or TiO2) to the surface of the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy in the cast state could overcome its poor oxygen resistance limitation without sacrificing its useful mechanical performance.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (up to 1000 °C) in an oxidizing atmosphere
generation.mechanism: Derived from materials-science principles, the coating acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, reducing the formation of oxide scales and preventing degradation of the alloy's mechanical properties. The coating's thickness and composition can be optimized to balance oxidation resistance and mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature oxidation resistance without significant degradation of mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength and tensile ductility)
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 25-1000 °C; Atmosphere: Oxidizing; Exposure time: Up to 100 hours; Mechanical loading: Tensile and compressive loads up to 500 MPa
generation.uncertainty: The effectiveness of the coating in improving oxidation resistance and maintaining mechanical performance may vary depending on the specific coating material, thickness, and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: High-temperature oxidation test with and without the coating, followed by tensile testing to evaluate mechanical properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated alloy exhibits significant degradation in mechanical properties (e.g., >20% reduction in yield strength or ductility) after high-temperature exposure, the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite processing challenges, and how do its microstructure, hardness, and corrosion resistance compare to traditional superalloys and arc-melted counterparts?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition of Nb, Mo, Ta, W powders with 99.9% purity). Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); parameters included hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, and a triple-pass remelting strategy (3x energy input) to achieve a linear energy density of 2.83 J/mm. Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
